summary:
Our "Sky over time" is a web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey images into timelapse videos of any patch of sky. Enter coordinates or pick a pre-existing example button such as Barnard's Star or the pulsating star R Draconis.
The tool downloads small cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA, cleans them (zodiacal light, cosmic rays, bad pixels), aligns them on one grid and plays them in order of observation date.
Markers from ESA's Gaia catalogue point out stars that move fast or vary in brightness, with plain language hints on what to watch for. SPHEREx data is powerful but hard for a layman to use. This tool makes a changing sky visible to students, teachers and curious people, without any specialised astronomy software.
details:
"Sky over time" shows how a small region of sky changes across SPHEREx's repeated visits. Users enter a position or choose an example target, load the images, and watch them play as a timelapse on a real timeline. Stars that move across the sky creep along a dashed path; variable stars brighten and fade. Hovering over a marker explains what the object is, how far away it is, and what to look for.

The backend searches IRSA's SIA2 service for every SPHEREx image covering the position, then reads only the needed region of each file from IRSA's public S3 mirror using HTTP range requests. Each cutout has the zodiacal light model subtracted, bad pixels hidden using the FLAGS bits (grouped into five switchable categories), and its background removed. Frames are resampled onto a common north-up grid using the full distortion model, with an interpolation that ignores masked pixels instead of smearing them. Users can average exposures, view differences from the median, and choose how missing pixels appear (transparent, filled from neighbours, filled from other visits, or black). Gaia DR3 is queried through ESA's TAP service for fast moving and variable stars, and CDS SIMBAD supplies names and object types. Markers are projected with the same coordinate system as the frames and follow each star's motion to the date of the frame on screen.

Benefits: It needs no specialised software install or knowledge of FITS files, and every control has a plain language explanation. It is honest about data quality: gaps are shown as gaps by default, and the page says when a setting invents data.

Intended impact: To make time domain astronomy and NASA's open SPHEREx data approachable for classrooms, outreach and curious people, and to help non experts find moving and variable objects themselves.

Tools: Python (FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, Requests) for the backend; React and Vite for the frontend; HTTP range requests on FITS files; ESA Gaia TAP and CDS SIMBAD TAP services.
